source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) The double-edged sword of recombination in breakthrough innovation
finding: They split 'breakthrough' into two things: cognitive novelty (a patent that starts a new topic) and economic value (forward citations). Distant and diverse recombination raises citations but lowers the chance of starting a new topic. Local search is what produces new topics.
numbers: Fullerene/nanotube patents, 100 LDA topics, 189 topic-originating patents (mean 1.89 per topic, median 1), 2,276 observations in the models, 109 patents in top 5% of 5-year forward citations. Competing mediation: total effect of distance/diversity on citations not significantly different from zero.
quote: distant and diverse recombinations ... pull in the opposite direction
limits: One technology domain (fullerenes, a general purpose technology). Topic model with 0.20 weight cutoff and 12-month window, tuned to three expert coders. Citation count is a noisy value proxy.
agent_relevance: Two selection targets that need different search modes. Wide recombination helps value; local deep search helps true novelty. Do not use one 'be more creative' dial.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) double-edged sword
finding: Novel ideas are worth more on average, but novelty is a weak filter for value. A topic-originating patent gets about 1.4 times the citations of an average patent.
numbers: Odds of being a top-5% cited patent rise by a factor of 1.7 for topic-originating patents. Probability of breakthrough citations 0.072 vs 0.024 for others (marginal effect 0.031). Only 20 of 189 topic-originating patents are also in the top 5% cited; topic-originating patents 5-year citations: mean 22.17, min 0, max 187.
limits: Same single-domain sample. 'Less than one percent' of patents are both cognitive and economic breakthroughs, so the base rate is tiny and estimates are noisy.
agent_relevance: Novel candidates are rarely the winners (about 11% overlap). Selection must not equate 'new' with 'good'; novelty needs a separate value check.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) double-edged sword
finding: The distance/diversity effect on citations was weak even in its own test: positive in direction, significant only for technological distance in the count model, and attenuated for the top-5% dummy. Robust to topic-originating threshold 0.15 and 0.25.
numbers: Effect of topic-originating dummy slightly lower at 0.25 and slightly higher at 0.15 cutoff, both still significant. Correlation of topic size with citations of originating patents: negative, not significant.
limits: Authors call the recombination-citation link a replication of earlier work but with different samples; the effect was not significant for diversity. The paper's own mechanism rests on a negative path (distance to novelty) from a single dataset.
agent_relevance: The famous 'distant recombination gives breakthroughs' claim is fragile when novelty is measured separately. Treat it as a hypothesis to test per task.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: High-impact papers pair a conventional core with a small dose of atypical journal combinations. Novelty alone or conventionality alone is not enough.
numbers: 17.9 million Web of Science papers. Hit = top 5% citations at 8 years. High median conventionality and high tail novelty: 9.11 hits per 100 (about 1.8 times the 5% background). One of the two only: 5.82 and 5.33 per 100. Neither: 2.05 per 100. Papers with tail novelty: 36.1, 39.8, 49.7% (by period); only 3.54% (1980s) and 2.67% (1990s) of papers had a negative median z score.
limits: Journal-pair novelty is a coarse proxy for idea novelty. Citation count as impact. Z-scores against randomized citation networks. Pattern held across 243 fields and for top 1% and top 10% definitions.
agent_relevance: A usable recipe for candidate generation: keep most of a solution conventional and add one distant element, rather than going fully exotic.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: Most science is highly conventional, and atypical combinations are rare. Teams are more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations into a familiar base.
numbers: Only about 41% of papers have a 10th-percentile z-score below zero. Teams 37.7% more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations into familiar knowledge. Of interdisciplinary journal pairs, 40.1% were novel (z below 0).
limits: Observational. Solo-author vs team comparison is not causal. Journal-level, not idea-level.
agent_relevance: Rare high-impact work is a tail event: most generated candidates will be conventional. Expect to need many samples, then a selector.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: Failed replication of Park et al. 2023. The reported decline in disruptiveness comes from database entries with zero references and CD5=1, hidden by a plotting bug (seaborn 0.11.2 dropped the top histogram bin).
numbers: Hidden outliers: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents with CD5 = 1. In SciSciNet (39,888,199 papers) 97% of CD5=1 papers have zero references; in PatentsView 78% of CD5=1 patents do. 93% of the papers and 98% of patents flagged as zero-reference do cite references in the original PDF/source. Removing the outliers removes the paper decline and substantially shrinks the patent decline. Randomly rewired networks reproduce the decline almost perfectly.
limits: A preprint reanalysis. It does not show disruptiveness is flat; it shows the headline decline is not identified by this data. Park et al. original used almost 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents.
agent_relevance: A cautionary case: a measure of 'disruption' depends on data quality. Any score our agent uses to pick breakthrough candidates needs a null model and a hand check of the extreme tail.

source: Leibel and Bornmann (2023/2024) What do we know about the disruption index in scientometrics?
finding: Review of the disruption index (DI1/CD index) and variants. Convergent validity evidence is mixed. DI1 is time-sensitive and biased by data coverage and by number of cited references. Variant DI5 does better than DI1 against Nobel and milestone benchmarks.
numbers: Deng and Zeng (2023), as reported in the review: average percentile ranks of milestone papers DI1 63.88 / DI5 83.59 / DI3% 92.72; Nobel Prize papers 69.67 / 86.91 / 92.40; review letters (should be low) 64.77 / 58.95 / 64.69. 87 PLR milestone papers (49 Nobel) and 1,671 Review of Modern Physics reviews.
limits: The review summarizes other studies, not new data. Evidence is mostly from physics and physiology/medicine benchmark sets.
agent_relevance: The measures we would use to judge 'breakthrough' disagree with each other. Use several indicators and treat any single one as a hint, not truth (fits G3, G4).

source: Leibel and Bornmann review (reporting Bornmann et al. 2020 factor analysis and reviewer-rating comparison)
finding: In a factor analysis of disruption indices, DI1 loaded negatively on citation impact, and disruption scores did not correlate with peer-review ratings. Several variants load on one dimension; DI1 does not.
quote: DI1 loads negatively on the citation dimension revealing that (a) high DI1 scores are related to low citation impact scores
numbers: As reported: no correlation between disruption scores and reviewers' star ratings. (Original study not opened this session; figures quoted via the review.)
limits: Second-hand via the review. Reviewer ratings are themselves noisy.
agent_relevance: Disruptive is not the same as highly cited or well rated. Do not let an LLM judge's rating stand in for breakthrough value.

source: Leibel and Bornmann review (reporting Leahey, Lee, Funk 2023 on types of novelty, and Shibayama and Wang 2020)
finding: Only some kinds of novelty go with disruption. In a Citation Classics dataset, new methods go with higher disruption; new theories and new results go with lower disruption scores. A survey study found disruption scores go with self-rated theoretical originality, not methodological originality. The two studies disagree on methods.
numbers: No effect sizes given in the review text read. Two studies, different designs and samples.
limits: Second-hand. The conflict (methods positive in one, null in the other) is unresolved.
agent_relevance: 'Novelty' is not one thing. An agent should state which kind it wants (new method, new theory, new result) before it searches.

source: Leibel and Bornmann review (reporting Ruan et al. 2021 and Sheng et al. 2023 on reference counts)
finding: The number of cited references changes disruption scores in a non-linear way. For papers with under 10 references the link is negative; above 10 it turns positive but small. Sign flips by period and citation window.
numbers: Ruan et al.: WoS articles 1954-2011 with at least 10 citations in 5 years, five disciplines; CSSCI 2000-2013. Sheng et al.: PubMed, 2001-2010, 5-year window positive; extended 10-year window gives weak negative.
limits: Second-hand. Shows the measure has a built-in artifact tied to paper length and style.
agent_relevance: Surface features (length, number of references) can fake 'novelty'. Normalize scores for length (as G5 already says).

source: Kelly, Papanikolaou, Seru, Taddy (2021) Measuring technological innovation over the long run (NBER w25266)
finding: A text-only score marks a significant patent as one that is different from the past and similar to the future. It predicts later citations years ahead and correlates with firm value, so rare high-impact work can be flagged from text with no citation data.
numbers: US patents 1840-2010. Moving from the median to the 90th percentile of the score gives 0.7 extra citations over 5 years and 1.5 over 10 years (median 2 and 3), same class, same firm, same year. One SD higher quality: 0.4 to 1.2 percentage-point higher patent value. Breakthrough = top 10% of the quality score after year fixed effects. One SD rise in the innovation index goes with 0.5 percent per year higher TFP growth (SD of TFP growth 1.8%).
limits: Working paper version (revised Feb 2020). Text similarity depends on word use and scan quality; handled with cohort fixed effects. Value for firms is not the same as scientific value.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-run, model-free scorer for 'novel and later influential' exists. This is the kind of selector G5 prefers over a model judge.

source: Gu and Krenn (2024/2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics via machine learning on evolving knowledge graphs
finding: A neural network on graph and citation features predicts which never-before-combined concept pairs will become high-impact three years later, before any paper exists. Not an LLM itself; built as a component for future idea-suggesting AI.
numbers: Knowledge graph from 21,165,421 papers, concept list from 2,444,442 papers; 141 features per pair (41 network, 100 impact). Test 2016 to 2019 and evaluation 2019 to 2022. AUC beyond 0.9 for most impact ranges (IR 1 to 200). Highest predicted pairs get over 3 orders of magnitude more citations than the average of 10 million pairs.
limits: Predicts citations of concept pairs, not quality of the work. Mostly physics, ML, and quantum fields. Authors say features need to be validated on other fields. High AUC is partly because most pairs are low-impact (class imbalance).
agent_relevance: Shows a code-side selector can rank unwritten ideas by later impact. Evidence for a scaffold that filters ideas with a trained counter instead of asking the LLM.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-agent ideas were rated more novel than expert human ideas, and slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 expert idea writers, 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews. Novelty (1-10): human ideas 4.84, AI ideas 5.64, AI ideas plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.01 with reviewer-level analysis; idea-level 4.86 vs 5.62 p=0.03, 5.78 p<0.01). Feasibility: human 6.61, AI 6.34, not significant. Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 (p=0.04), 5.46 (p<0.01). Overall 4.68 vs 4.85 (n.s.), 5.34 (p=0.04). Style normalization: human judges got 50% accuracy telling AI from human.
limits: Ideas only, not executed. NLP topics (7 topics), one prompting-style agent. Reviewer agreement is low (56.1%). Human writers were not given their best idea, per the authors' discussion.
agent_relevance: Novelty looks cheap for an LLM. The hard part is what comes after: picking the ideas that survive execution.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Scaling up idea generation hits a diversity wall, and LLMs cannot judge ideas reliably. Both are direct selection problems.
numbers: From 4,000 generated seed ideas only about 5% (200) remain after deduplication at cosine similarity 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Reviewer agreement (top vs bottom 25%) among experts: 56.1%; NeurIPS 2021 66.0%; ICLR 2024 71.9%; random 50%. LLM judges against the human mean: GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3%, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Judge accuracy measured against noisy expert scores on 100+ ideas per side. Models of mid-2024.
agent_relevance: Directly supports G5: no LLM judge for picking breakthrough ideas. Also: more samples from one model repeats itself (G4).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap: execution outcomes of LLM-generated versus human research ideas
finding: Follow-up with execution. 43 experts each spent over 100 hours implementing a random idea (AI or human) and wrote a 4-page paper. After execution, AI ideas lose their novelty edge and even flip below human ideas.
numbers: N=43 projects (19 human, 24 AI), 58 reviewers, 181 ideas pre-execution (85 human, 96 AI). Score drops after execution, human vs AI: novelty -0.010 vs -1.049; excitement +0.078 vs -1.760; effectiveness -0.052 vs -1.879. Gap difference (human minus AI) 1.039, 1.835, 1.827, 1.348 on novelty, excitement, effectiveness, overall; FDR p=0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004. Effectiveness after execution: AI 4.13 vs human 4.78; excitement 3.90 vs 4.48 (not significant).
limits: Small N=43 executed projects; NLP-only, one agent. Rank flip not statistically significant when ideas are treated as units. Ideation vs execution scores correlate weakly; for AI ideas the excitement correlation was moderately negative.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI test of the 'seems novel but is not a breakthrough' problem. Ideas must be tested by running them, not by rating them (G2, G3).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: Its automated reviewer is tuned to ICLR scores and reaches human-level agreement, so a model reviewer can match the weak human signal. The AI Scientist's own novelty check uses a literature search flag.
numbers: Reviewer on ICLR 2022 OpenReview: 65% balanced accuracy vs 66% for humans (NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment). F1 0.57 vs 0.49, AUC 0.65 for both. Correlation of two human reviewers' scores 0.14 vs 0.18 for LLM score against the average human score. Best reviewer: GPT-4o with 5 rounds self-reflection and 5 ensembled reviews.
limits: Peer-review acceptance is a weak target, as the 56.1% to 72% agreement numbers in b14 show. Does not test breakthrough impact. Self-assessed novelty scores from the model tend to be over-optimistic.
agent_relevance: Matching a noisy human reviewer is not the same as spotting rare high-impact work. Do not read 'human-level' as 'good at breakthroughs'.

source: Lin, Frey, Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas
finding: Remote teams are less likely to make disruptive papers or patents than on-site teams, across fields, periods and team sizes. Remote teams do late-stage technical work; on-site teams do conceptual work like conceiving ideas.
numbers: 20 million papers (1960-2020) and 4 million patents (1976-2020). Probability of disruption P(D>0) falls from 28% to 22% for papers and from 67% to 55% for patents as distance goes from 0 km to over 600 km (p<0.001). Within-team measure: P(D>0) 20.4% to 19.5% for papers and 58.2% to 56.5% for patents (a 3-4% relative penalty). Collaboration over 2,500 km rose from 2% to 15% (papers) and 3% to 9% (patents).
limits: Uses D-score (disruption index), so it inherits the data-artifact worry in b06. Observational. Gap is relatively small in the within-team version.
agent_relevance: Weak analogy only: splitting conceptual work from execution across agents may cut the integrating step. Keep concept formation in one thread.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) double-edged sword
finding: The authors flag creativity theory: skills to produce novel ideas and skills to select and sell valuable ones are weakly related at best. This is the source of the novelty-versus-value split.
numbers: Cites Sternberg and O'Hara 1999. Citation counts correlate noisily with value (Bessen 2008); better proxies include patent renewals, multi-jurisdiction filing and stock value.
limits: A theoretical claim carried into the paper, not tested in it.
agent_relevance: Generation and selection are different skills. Our scaffold should give them to different parts (model generates, code selects).

source: Kelly et al. (2021) Measuring technological innovation over the long run
finding: Text-based breakthrough flags beat citation counts at finding known major inventions of the 19th and 20th centuries, by the authors' check against a list built by research assistants. Compared with forward-citation breakthroughs it uses the same top-10% cut.
numbers: Breakthrough defined as top 10% of the quality distribution with a 10-year forward window; alternative defined as top 10% by forward citations. Comparison table of known inventions is in the paper; exact hit counts not captured in this read.
limits: The known-breakthrough list is hand-built; hindsight bias is possible. Text similarity cannot see non-text influence.
agent_relevance: Gives a base-rate approach: define breakthrough as a stated top slice of a code-computed score, and report overlap with a second definition.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) double-edged sword
finding: Inventor experience is the only recombination-related control that is significant for both topic-originating status and citations.
numbers: Positive and significant experience effect on both novelty (path A) and citations. Significance of other controls attenuated in the top-5% dummy model because of lower outcome variance.
limits: Cannot tell if experience acts through deep field knowledge (foundational view) or recombination skill (tension view); the authors say so.
agent_relevance: Expertise (deep prior knowledge) matters for novelty. Retrieval of domain knowledge before ideation is a plausible lever; untested here.

source: Holst et al. (2024) Dataset artefacts and declining disruptiveness
finding: The original robustness checks missed the artifact. A regression adjustment cannot fix a discontinuity (CD index jumps to 1 when a paper has zero references and at least one citer).
numbers: Random citation rewiring reproduces the decline almost exactly, so the original Monte Carlo null did not separate real decline from the data structure.
limits: Authors state their own result is about the data artifact, not a proof that science is not getting less disruptive.
agent_relevance: A null model that shares the artifact proves nothing. Our G3 asks for a held-out check that the fit did not create the pass.

source: Leibel and Bornmann review (best-practice conclusions)
finding: The review concludes disruption indices should not yet be used in research evaluation practice. More work on the theoretical definition of disruption is needed first.
numbers: No single number; conclusion drawn from the review of validity studies (Nobel, milestone, expert-tag, and reviewer-rating tests).
limits: Written by scientometrics authors who also propose variants; some self-interest in variant papers.
agent_relevance: No agreed definition of 'breakthrough'. The scaffold should set its own operational definition per task and check it.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: The study design controls for confounders: same topics, same template, LLM style normalizer, and a human check that no content changed. Even so, reviewers rated the AI ideas higher on novelty and excitement but did not differ on feasibility or overall (unreranked).
numbers: Overall score: human 4.68 vs AI 4.85 (p=1.00 after correction); with human rerank 5.34 (p=0.04). Human-reranking of the AI ideas raised every score a little (novelty 5.64 to 5.81).
limits: Multiple-comparison correction used. Overall score for plain AI ideas was not significant.
agent_relevance: A human-in-the-loop selector helped a bit. An automated selector tied to execution may do better; this is not measured.

source: Si et al. (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: Pre-execution ratings predict post-execution ratings weakly. Rating ideas on paper is a poor predictor of how the executed project is judged.
numbers: Correlation between ideation and execution scores is weak in most cases; for AI ideas the excitement correlation is moderately negative (appendix D, exact values not captured).
limits: N=43 projects. Executors could change the idea; some did.
agent_relevance: If our agent rates a plan before running it, expect weak signal. Prefer cheap partial execution (a small test) as the selector.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: The conventional-plus-novel pattern holds across time periods, definitions of a hit, and fields. Robustness checks cover other decades (1950-2000), hit = top 1% or top 10%, and 243 fields.
numbers: Paper reports the difference in hit probabilities across the four groups as significant; the caption lists 6.7%, 23%, 26% and 44% for the compared contrasts (relative differences).
limits: A citation-lag claim sometimes attributed to this paper was not found in the text I read, so it is not recorded.
agent_relevance: The pattern is stable, so a conventional-core-plus-one-novel-element recipe is not an artifact of one decade or one cutoff.

source: Gu and Krenn (2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics
finding: They define 'impact range' thresholds: a pair counts as high-impact if it gets at least IR citations in three years, from IR=1 up to IR=200. They train per threshold and report quality for each.
numbers: IR from 1 to 200. AUC beyond 0.9 for most thresholds. Evaluated on about 10 million unconnected pairs; binned in 20 groups of 5%, where the top bin average is more than 1,000 times the all-pairs average.
limits: Binary classification on citation thresholds; no human-rated quality check; class imbalance inflates AUC.
agent_relevance: Choosing the threshold changes the question. State the cutoff for 'breakthrough' before measuring (G3-style pre-registration).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: Authors admit a model's own novelty, interest and feasibility scores run over-optimistic, and Llama 3.1 405B could not follow the reviewer output format.
numbers: Not a numeric result; the paper notes over-optimism bias in idea scoring and reports the final reviewer as GPT-4o.
limits: Qualitative statement in the paper; judged mostly on ML templates.
agent_relevance: Self-assessed novelty is inflated; consistent with G5 (never let the model grade its own idea without a check).

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) double-edged sword
finding: The paper offers an organizational reading: firms must hold both deep knowledge (for new topics) and long-jump search (for value). Not tested as an intervention.
numbers: No intervention study. Fullerene general-purpose-technology generality index above 0.6 for 1990-2000, about 50 percent higher than reported for other patents (Hall et al. 2001).
limits: Setting chosen because it should yield many breakthroughs; may not generalize to incremental fields.
agent_relevance: A two-phase design (deep local search to find a new angle, then wide search to test its value) is suggested, not proven.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (as discussed in Lin et al. 2023 and Leibel and Bornmann 2023)
finding: Nature page could not be opened (redirect to login). Second-hand: small teams and solo researchers are more likely to disrupt; large teams develop. Lin et al. (opened) cite it and test the remote-team version.
numbers: Not read directly. Cited in b17 as the basis for the D-score and team-structure link.
limits: Not opened. Also depends on the disruption index, so the same artifact worry as b06 may apply.
agent_relevance: Weak: small independent threads may disrupt more than one big pooled effort. Untested for agents.

source: Park, Leahey, Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time
finding: Nature page could not be opened. As described by Holst et al. (opened): CD index analysis of almost 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents found a decline. Holst et al. say that decline comes from zero-reference records.
numbers: Not read directly. Figures of 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents come from the Holst et al. abstract.
limits: Not opened. Contested by b06; a reply by the original authors was not found in this session.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'science is getting less disruptive' as a premise for the design.
